title: One bootmaker, two legal persons
subtitle: Salomon and the doctrine of separate legal personality
objectives: State the rule in Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd that a validly incorporated company is a legal person distinct from its members
Identify the practical consequences of separate personality: limited liability, perpetual succession, and the company's own capacity to hold property and make contracts
Apply the separate-personality principle to a new fact pattern, correctly distinguishing the company's assets and liabilities from those of its members and directors

leadingAuthorities.citation: Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd [1897] AC 22
leadingAuthorities.role: Establishes that a validly incorporated company is a distinct legal person from its shareholders, even where one person owns nearly all the shares and controls it completely
Statutory confirmation that registration brings the company into existence as a body corporate from the date stated on the certificate of incorporation

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Everything else in this module — limited liability, directors' duties, shareholder remedies, insolvency exposure — is built on top of one idea: the company is not the same legal person as the people who own or run it. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can state the rule — this lesson checks whether you can spot when it's being tested without being named.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans towards scenario questions: expect facts about a struggling business, not a request to define 'separate legal personality'.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and take it slowly — the Salomon facts and holding are the foundation the rest of this module assumes you already know cold.

overview.hook: Aron Salomon sold his own boot-and-leather business to a company he had just created, took nearly all its shares himself, and lent the company money secured on its assets. When the business failed, the unsecured creditors argued the company was a fiction — that Salomon and his company were, in substance, the same person, and he should pay their debts personally. Two courts agreed with them. The House of Lords didn't. What it said next created the single most important idea in company law, and this lesson is about what that idea actually means once you get past the slogan.

parts.heading: A bootmaker, his family, and a company of seven
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the story before naming the doctrine
body: Aron Salomon had run a successful leather and boot-manufacturing business as a sole trader for around thirty years. In 1892, on the advice of his solicitors and following the fashion of the day, he incorporated it: he formed 'A Salomon & Co Ltd' under the Companies Act 1862, which — like the Companies Act 2006 does today — required a company to have a minimum number of subscribing members.

Salomon sold his existing business to the new company for a price of around £39,000. He was paid partly in cash, partly in 20,000 £1 shares, and partly in a debenture — a secured loan of £10,000, charged over the company's assets, that ranked ahead of the company's other, unsecured creditors if it ever failed. To satisfy the statutory minimum, Salomon's wife and five of his children each took one further share, nominally, so the company had exactly the seven members the Act required. Salomon himself held 20,001 of the 20,007 issued shares and was, in substance, running the same business as before, now through a corporate shell he controlled entirely.

The company struggled almost immediately amid a slump in the boot trade, and went into liquidation within a couple of years. Its assets, once Salomon was paid out as a secured debenture-holder, were not enough to pay the unsecured trade creditors anything at all. The liquidator, on their behalf, sued Salomon personally — arguing that the company had really been Salomon's agent or trustee all along, that incorporation had been a device to defeat creditors, and that he should be made to indemnify the company for its debts.

components.caseName: Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd
components.factsShort: A sole trader incorporated his business, took almost all the shares and a secured debenture, and the company later failed leaving unsecured creditors unpaid.
components.ratioShort: A company validly formed under the Act is a legal person separate from its subscribers, whatever their motive for incorporating and however completely one person controls it.

expanded.facts: Aron Salomon sold his sole-trader boot business to a newly incorporated company in which he held almost all the shares, with one nominal share each held by his wife and five children to meet the statutory minimum membership. He also took a debenture secured over the company's assets. When the company failed, its unsecured creditors would receive nothing once Salomon was repaid as a secured creditor. The liquidator argued the company was Salomon's agent or a sham, and sought to make him personally liable for its debts.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The House of Lords held unanimously that the company had been validly formed under the Companies Act 1862: the statute required seven members holding at least one share each, and said nothing about those members needing to be independent of one another or to hold shares in any particular proportion. Lord Macnaghten's speech is the one students quote: the company 'is at law a different person altogether from the subscribers'; and though it may be that after incorporation the business is precisely what it was before, and the same persons are managers, 'the company is not in law the agent of the subscribers or trustee for them'. Motive for incorporating was irrelevant to the question of whether a valid company existed.
expanded.significance: Salomon is the founding case of modern company law. It settles, as a matter of binding authority, that incorporation creates a genuinely new legal person — not a legal fiction that courts can look behind whenever it produces an inconvenient result for creditors. Everything from limited liability to today's veil-piercing doctrine (the subject of the next lesson) exists in the shadow this case casts.

interaction.prompt: In Salomon, did the House of Lords accept the liquidator's argument that the company was really just Salomon's agent?
options: No — the House of Lords held the company was a separate legal person, not Salomon's agent
Yes — the House of Lords agreed the company was Salomon's agent and made him personally liable
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The Court of Appeal and the trial judge had both accepted something close to the agency argument — the House of Lords unanimously reversed them.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at how the case actually ended. Two lower courts sided with the liquidator; the House of Lords reversed them and rejected the agency argument outright.

parts.heading: What 'separate legal personality' actually means
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: 'The company is a separate legal person' is easy to recite and genuinely hard to internalise, because in a small company the same humans are doing everything the company appears to do — signing the contracts, running the bank account, making the decisions. The doctrine asks you to hold two facts in mind at once: the natural persons involved and the company itself are legally distinct, even when they are, practically speaking, the same people acting through a corporate form.

Once a company is validly incorporated, it becomes what lawyers call a body corporate: an artificial legal person, entirely separate from its members (the shareholders) and from anyone who manages it (the directors). It can own property in its own name, sue and be sued in its own name, enter contracts in its own name, and incur debts that are its debts — not the debts of the people behind it. None of that depended on the size of the company or on how many 'real' shareholders it had; a company owned almost entirely by one person is exactly as separate as one with thousands of shareholders spread across the world.

This is worth stating precisely, because exam answers lose marks for vague paraphrase: separate legal personality is not the same thing as limited liability, and it is not the same thing as the corporate veil (which is about when courts will disregard personality — the next lesson's subject). Personality is the underlying legal status; limited liability, perpetual succession and the rest are consequences that flow from it.

components.definition: The principle that a validly incorporated company is a legal person in its own right, distinct from its members and directors — capable of owning property, contracting, suing and being sued, and owing its own debts, independently of the individuals who own or run it.

components.label: What Salomon actually decided
points: A company formed in compliance with the statutory requirements is validly incorporated, whatever the incorporator's motive for forming it
The company is, from the moment of incorporation, a legal person separate from its subscribers — not their agent or trustee
This is true even where one person holds almost all the shares and controls the company completely

A secured creditor of the company (here, Salomon under his debenture) ranks ahead of unsecured creditors on liquidation — the debenture was valid precisely because the company was a separate debtor from Salomon himself

interaction.prompt: Put the procedural history of Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd in order.
items: The trial judge finds the company was Salomon's agent and orders him to indemnify it
The Court of Appeal upholds that decision on similar reasoning
The House of Lords hears the appeal
The House of Lords unanimously reverses, holding the company a separate legal person
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the arc worth remembering: two courts ruled against Salomon before the House of Lords overturned them both and set the doctrine that has governed ever since.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — Salomon lost twice, at trial and in the Court of Appeal, before the House of Lords reversed both lower courts and established the modern rule.

parts.heading: The statute behind the doctrine
parts.voice: statute-first — works from the text outward
body: Salomon is a common-law decision interpreting the Companies Act 1862, but the underlying statutory mechanism survives, almost unchanged in substance, in the Companies Act 2006. Section 16 is the provision that actually creates the legal person the rest of this module assumes exists.

Section 16(1) provides that on the registrar issuing a certificate of incorporation, the requirements of the Act as to registration are deemed to have been complied with. Section 16(2) — the part students are expected to know — then does the real work: it states that from the date on the certificate, the subscribers to the memorandum, together with anyone who later becomes a member, are a body corporate by the registered name.

Notice what this provision does not require: it says nothing about the company needing 'real' independent shareholders, a minimum level of trading activity, or any particular purpose behind incorporating. A company formed to protect one trader from personal liability, or to keep a family business's assets separate from a family member's personal creditors, is formed exactly as validly as one formed by a large public company with thousands of unconnected investors.

components.text: (1) The registration of a company has the following effects as from the date of incorporation. (2) As from the date of incorporation mentioned in the certificate of incorporation, the subscribers to the memorandum, together with such other persons as may from time to time become members of the company, are a body corporate by the name stated in the certificate of incorporation.
elements: Effect runs from the date on the certificate of incorporation
The original subscribers, plus anyone who later becomes a member
Become a body corporate (a legal person) by the registered name
No requirement of independence between members, or of any particular purpose for incorporating

interaction.prompt: Under s 16(2) of the Companies Act 2006, from what moment does a company become a body corporate?
options: From the date stated on its certificate of incorporation
From the date its first annual accounts are filed
From the date the company starts trading
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Legal personality attaches precisely at incorporation, as certified by the registrar — not at the point the company begins doing business.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look at the wording again: s 16(2) fixes the moment as 'the date of incorporation mentioned in the certificate of incorporation' — trading activity and accounts filing come later and are irrelevant to when personality begins.

parts.heading: Four consequences that follow from one idea
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Separate legal personality is the axiom; everything else in this lesson is a theorem derived from it. Four consequences matter most for the rest of the module, and each has tripped up generations of students who understand the headline rule but not what it actually implies on a fact pattern.

Limited liability is the consequence most people reach for first, but it is worth being precise: it is the members' liability that is limited (typically to the amount, if any, unpaid on their shares), not the company's. The company itself is always fully liable for its own debts, without limit — it simply may not have enough assets to pay them, which is a different problem entirely. Perpetual succession means the company continues in existence regardless of changes in its membership: shareholders can die, resign, sell their shares or be bought out, and the company itself is entirely unaffected, still bound by the same contracts and still owing the same debts. Because it is a separate person, the company can also hold property in its own name — company assets belong to the company, not (even loosely, even proportionately) to its shareholders, who own shares in the company rather than a share of its assets. And the company can contract in its own name, including with its own controlling shareholder or director: a director who is also an employee is, for many legal purposes, owed duties by 'someone else' — the company — even though they may run it single-handedly.

Exam fact patterns test these consequences separately, because students who have only memorised 'limited liability' often misapply it to questions that are really about perpetual succession or the company's separate ownership of assets.

components.title: From separate personality to its consequences
components.description: How the single idea in Salomon produces the four consequences tested across this module.

nodes.label: The company is a separate legal person (Salomon; CA 2006 s 16(2))
Limited liability: members' exposure is capped, not the company's
Perpetual succession: the company survives changes in membership
Separate ownership: company assets belong to the company, not its members
Separate capacity to contract, including with its own controllers

components.textAlternative: Separate legal personality, as established in Salomon and confirmed by s 16(2) of the Companies Act 2006, produces four consequences: limited liability (the members' exposure is capped, not the company's own liability for its debts), perpetual succession (the company survives changes in who its members are), separate ownership of property (company assets belong to the company itself, not proportionately to its shareholders), and a separate capacity to contract, including with the very individuals who control it.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact below that illustrates perpetual succession, rather than limited liability or separate ownership of property.
interaction.scenarioText: Rania is the sole shareholder and director of a small design company. She sells all her shares to a buyer and retires. The company continues trading under the same name, still bound by its existing office lease and supplier contracts, entirely unaffected by the change in who owns it.
tappableSpans: sells all her shares to a buyer
continues trading under the same name
entirely unaffected by the change in who owns it
interaction.correctSpan: entirely unaffected by the change in who owns it
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's perpetual succession in one phrase: the company's existence, contracts and obligations carry on regardless of who its members happen to be at any given moment.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the fact that describes the company's continuity despite the change of ownership, not the change of ownership itself. Perpetual succession is about what stays the same for the company, not about the share sale.

parts.heading: Why this is the axiom of the whole module
parts.voice: reflective — closes the lesson by justifying its own place in the syllabus
body: It's worth being blunt about why this lesson sits first in the module. Directors' duties only make sense once you accept that a director owes duties to a legal person distinct from themselves and from the shareholders. Shareholder remedies only make sense once you accept that shareholders do not own the company's assets directly, and so need a separate legal mechanism to complain about how those assets are managed. Insolvency law's entire structure — the pecking order of secured, preferential and unsecured creditors that determined Salomon's own outcome — depends on the company being a distinct debtor with its own estate.

None of this means separate personality is absolute or beyond challenge. Courts have, in a narrow and tightly controlled set of circumstances, been prepared to look behind the corporate form — and the next lesson is entirely about when, and on what basis, they will actually do that. But it is a genuinely narrow exception to a rule the House of Lords stated as close to absolute in 1897, and it remains good law today: separate personality is the default, not something a claimant can simply assert around.

components.definition: The metaphorical barrier separate legal personality creates between a company and the individuals who own or run it — a preview of a concept this module returns to in the next lesson, on the narrow circumstances in which courts will disregard it.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that a shareholder in a company limited by shares is personally liable, without limit, for that company's unpaid debts?
sliderLabels: Definitely not liable (beyond any unpaid share amount)
interaction.correctPosition: Definitely not liable (beyond any unpaid share amount)
interaction.explanation: Not liable, beyond whatever (if anything) remains unpaid on their shares. The company itself is fully liable for its own debts without limit; it is the member's exposure, not the company's, that limited liability caps — and Salomon's own creditors could not simply reach past the company to him.

testPool.prompt: State the core rule established in Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd.
acceptableAnswers: a company is a separate legal person from its members
the company is a distinct legal person, not the agent of its subscribers
testPool.modelAnswer: A validly incorporated company is a legal person separate from its members, even where one person holds almost all the shares and controls it completely; it is not the agent or trustee of its subscribers.

testPool.prompt: In Salomon, whose debenture ranked ahead of the unsecured trade creditors when the company was wound up?
options: Aron Salomon's
The trade creditors held equal ranking with Salomon

testPool.prompt: Which of the following did the House of Lords in Salomon treat as irrelevant to whether the company was validly incorporated?
options: Whether the statutory minimum number of members was met
Salomon's motive for incorporating the business
Whether the company was properly registered with the registrar
testPool.trapExplanation: Students often assume a company formed mainly to obtain limited liability is somehow suspect. Salomon rejects that instinct directly: motive for incorporating has no bearing on validity, provided the statutory formalities (membership, registration) were actually satisfied.

testPool.prompt: Order the events in Aron Salomon's incorporation of his business.
items: Salomon runs a boot and leather business as a sole trader
He incorporates A Salomon & Co Ltd with six family members as fellow subscribers
He sells his existing business to the new company, taking shares and a secured debenture
The company later fails, and its unsecured creditors are left unpaid

testPool.prompt: Under s 16(2) of the Companies Act 2006, who becomes a member of the newly incorporated body corporate?
options: The subscribers to the memorandum, together with anyone who later becomes a member
Only the person who paid the registration fee
Only shareholders holding more than 50% of the issued shares

testPool.prompt: In the extract below from Lord Macnaghten's speech in Salomon, highlight the sentence that most precisely states the ratio.
testPool.passage: It has become the fashion to call companies of this class 'one man companies.' That is a taking nickname, but it does not help one much in the way of argument. The company is at law a different person altogether from the subscribers to the memorandum; and, though it may be that after incorporation the business is precisely what it was before, and the same persons are managers, and the same hands receive the profits, the company is not in law the agent of the subscribers or trustee for them.
testPool.ratioSentence: The company is at law a different person altogether from the subscribers to the memorandum

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that shows separate legal personality, rather than limited liability, is the point at issue in this scenario.
testPool.scenarioText: A supplier delivers goods to a company and is never paid. The company owned a warehouse of stock, but that stock belonged to the company itself, not proportionately to its two shareholders, and the supplier has no claim against the shareholders' own personal property.
tappableSpans: that stock belonged to the company itself, not proportionately to its two shareholders
no claim against the shareholders' own personal property
testPool.correctSpan: that stock belonged to the company itself, not proportionately to its two shareholders
testPool.explanation: This is the separate-ownership consequence: company property belongs to the company as a distinct legal person, not to shareholders in proportion to their shareholding — a different point from the liability cap, even though both often appear in the same fact pattern.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario best illustrates perpetual succession?
testPool.scenarioA: A company's sole director dies suddenly; the company itself continues to exist, still bound by its existing contracts, while new directors are appointed to run it.
testPool.scenarioB: A company is sued by a customer for a faulty product, and the customer wins damages that must be paid out of company funds rather than the director's personal savings.
testPool.explanation: A is perpetual succession: the company's existence and obligations are unaffected by the death or departure of the individuals involved. B illustrates a different consequence — the company's separate liability for its own debts and judgments, which underlies limited liability for its members.

testPool.prompt: Priya is the sole shareholder and director of a consultancy company. The company enters a supply contract with a printer, on company letterhead, signed 'for and on behalf of [Company] Ltd.' The printer later wants to sue Priya personally when the company cannot pay. Applying Salomon, can the printer do so on the basis of separate personality alone?
options: No — the contract was made by the company, a separate legal person, and Priya is not personally a party to it merely because she owns and runs the company
Yes — since Priya owns virtually all the shares, she and the company are treated as the same person
Yes — any director who signs a contract is automatically personally liable on it
testPool.explanation: This is Salomon applied directly: sole ownership and control do not collapse the company into its controller. The contract is the company's, and the printer's remedy (absent some separate basis for personal liability) lies against the company, not against Priya.

testPool.prompt: Under s 16(2) of the Companies Act 2006, does a company need independent, unconnected shareholders to be validly incorporated?
options: No — the section imposes no such requirement
Yes — at least a majority of members must be unconnected to each other

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that 'limited liability' and 'separate legal personality' mean the same thing?
sliderLabels: They're distinct — personality is the underlying status, limited liability is one consequence of it
testPool.correctPosition: They're distinct — personality is the underlying status, limited liability is one consequence of it
testPool.explanation: Distinct. Separate legal personality is the underlying doctrine from Salomon and s 16(2); limited liability is one of several consequences that flow from it, alongside perpetual succession and the company's separate capacity to hold property and contract.

testPool.prompt: Tomas is the sole director and 100% shareholder of a small catering company. The company takes out a business loan and later defaults. The lender wants to sue Tomas personally for the shortfall, arguing that since he owns and controls the whole company, he and it are 'effectively the same thing.' Analyse whether the lender's argument succeeds on the principle in Salomon alone.
factsToOrder: The company, not Tomas personally, took out the loan
Tomas owns 100% of the shares and is the sole director
The lender argues Tomas and the company are 'effectively the same thing'
The company has defaulted and cannot repay

scaffolds.support: Full model answer shown, mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student applies it to the facts and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full analysis unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Tomas can be made personally liable for the company's loan on the basis that he owns and controls it entirely.
modelAnswer.rule: Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd establishes that a validly incorporated company is a separate legal person from its members, whatever their motive for incorporating, and however completely one person controls it; the company is not the agent or trustee of its controller.
modelAnswer.application: Tomas's complete ownership and control mirror Salomon's own position almost exactly. The loan was made to the company, a distinct legal person, and Tomas is not automatically a party to it or liable for it simply because he owns all the shares and runs the business day to day.
modelAnswer.conclusion: On Salomon alone, the lender's argument fails: sole ownership and control do not, by themselves, make Tomas personally liable for the company's debt.

testPool.prompt: A student writes: 'Salomon shows that one-man companies are legally suspect and courts will usually disregard them if the sole owner benefits unfairly.' What is wrong with this statement?
options: It correctly summarises the ratio of Salomon
It states the opposite of the actual holding — Salomon confirms one-person-controlled companies are just as validly separate as any other
It confuses Salomon with a case about directors' duties rather than personality
testPool.trapExplanation: This is the most common misreading of the case: students sometimes remember the facts (a one-man company, unpaid creditors) and infer the House of Lords was suspicious of the arrangement. It wasn't — the whole point of the decision is that the company's validity and separateness do not depend on how concentrated its ownership is.

testPool.prompt: Name the four consequences of separate legal personality covered in this lesson.
acceptableAnswers: limited liability, perpetual succession, separate ownership of property, separate capacity to contract
limited liability, perpetual succession, the company can own property, the company can contract in its own name
testPool.modelAnswer: Limited liability of members, perpetual succession of the company, the company's separate ownership of its own property, and the company's separate capacity to enter contracts, including with its own controllers.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating a one-person-controlled company as somehow less 'real' or less separate than a widely-held one. Salomon rejects that instinct outright: complete ownership and control by a single individual do not collapse the company into that individual — a distinction the next lesson's veil-piercing doctrine narrows only slightly, and only in tightly defined circumstances.
